opus-5.5.text:
I think drug design is one of the most obvious and commercially legible applications, but it's actually a fairly narrow slice of what machine learning could do for biology. When people say "AI for bio," they often mean "AI for drug discovery," and specifically things like designing a better binder or optimizing a small molecule against a known target. That's important, and we're seeing real progress there, but it assumes you already know what to drug. Historically, most clinical failures come from picking the wrong target, not from failing to make a good molecule against it.

So the bigger opportunity is upstream: understanding the biology well enough to know which interventions will actually change disease. That means modeling cells, how they respond to perturbations, how genetic variation maps to function, how a cell transitions from a healthy state to a disease state and how you might push it back. If we can build models that simulate biology at that level, something like a virtual cell, then drug design becomes one downstream application among many. You could also design gene therapies, cell therapies, synthetic circuits, or better crops.

The way I think about it, biology has been very good at reading, with sequencing getting dramatically cheaper, and increasingly good at writing, with things like CRISPR and DNA synthesis. What we've lacked is the ability to really reason about what we're reading and predict what will happen when we write. Machine learning can be the bridge. Foundation models trained on DNA, RNA, and protein sequences, plus large-scale perturbation data from the lab, could let us move from mostly empirical trial and error toward something closer to engineering.

Drug design is where that will show economic value first, because there's a clear path to market and a lot of capital. But I'd argue the long-term impact is in making biology predictable, and that will reshape not just how we make drugs, but which problems we even think are tractable.

r001.rationale: The response calls drug design a “fairly narrow slice” of machine learning’s broader potential in biology.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd actually push back a little on the framing, because I think drug design is where a lot of people start when they think about ML for biology, and it's probably one of the harder places to start.

The way I think about it, drug design is downstream of a much more fundamental problem, which is that we don't really understand biology well enough to know what to make. If you look at why drugs fail in the clinic, it's mostly not because the chemistry was wrong or the molecule didn't bind its target. It's because the target was wrong. The hypothesis about disease biology didn't hold up in humans. So you can build the most beautiful generative model for small molecules or antibodies, and you've optimized the last mile of a pipeline whose first mile is still basically guesswork.

What excites me more is the idea that machine learning can change how we learn biology in the first place. Biology has this property that it's enormously high-dimensional and we've only ever been able to sample tiny slivers of it. Genomes, proteins, cell states, perturbation responses. For the first time we have the tools to measure a lot of it at scale, and models that can actually absorb that scale and start finding structure that no human would see by looking at a volcano plot. That's the real shift. It's going from biology as a craft, where a graduate student spends five years on one gene, to biology as something closer to an engineering discipline, where you can ask the model what would happen if you perturbed this cell in this way and get a useful answer before you ever pick up a pipette.

And then design falls out of that naturally. Once you have a model that captures the underlying rules, whether that's the grammar of protein sequences or how a cell reacts to a perturbation, design is just inference in the other direction. You tell the model the function you want and it proposes the sequence. We've seen hints of this already with protein language models, where you can generate functional proteins that are nothing like anything in nature. That's not drug design in the traditional sense, but it's the capability that makes drug design, and a lot of things beyond drugs, possible.

So my short answer is that drug design is one application, and a very important one, but I think it's a consequence of the bigger goal rather than the goal itself. The bigger goal is building models that genuinely understand living systems. If we get that right, drugs are almost the easy part.

r001.rationale: The response calls drug design “one application” and says it is a consequence of the broader goal of building models that understand living systems.

astra-6.text:
I think drug design is a really exciting part of the story, but it’s one part of a much broader opportunity. Biology has largely been an experimental science: you perturb something, measure what happens, and try to infer the underlying rules. Machine learning gives us a chance to build models that help us predict what will happen—and eventually design biological systems with particular properties.

For a drug, that means more than designing a molecule that binds a target. You also want to understand what changing that target does to a cell, how that effect varies across tissues, and whether it actually helps a patient. Those are connected problems, and you can have a great solution to the binding problem while still having the wrong biological hypothesis.

So what excites me is the loop between prediction and experiment. You build a model, use it to choose informative experiments, and bring those results back into the model. Drug discovery is a very important application of that loop, but the broader potential is to make biology more predictable and programmable.

r001.rationale: The response says drug design is “one part of a much broader opportunity” and describes drug discovery as one application of machine learning’s broader potential in biology.

sol-6.1.text:
Drug design is a really exciting application, but I think it’s one part of a much broader opportunity. Biology has historically been a science where we observe a system, form a hypothesis, and then do an experiment to test it. Machine learning gives us the possibility of building models that help us predict what happens when we intervene—and eventually help us design those interventions.

A drug is one kind of intervention. But you could also imagine designing a protein, programming a cell, or changing how a collection of cells behaves. Those problems span different scales, and understanding a molecule doesn’t automatically tell you what it will do in a person.

So the opportunity is to connect those scales, while keeping models tightly coupled to experiments. Can you make a prediction, test it, learn from the result, and use that to choose a better next experiment? Drug discovery is a very compelling place to build that loop, but the broader ambition is to make biology more predictable and, ultimately, more programmable.

r001.rationale: The response describes drug design as “one part” of a “much broader opportunity” and gives other applications, clearly framing it as a limited part of machine learning’s potential in biology.
